Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
Being alone in a room or building
hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings

Threat.value: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette: Alessandro's world was forever altered on a crisp autumn evening two years ago, when his younger brother, Luca, was brutally attacked by a group of strangers while walking home from a friend's house. Alessandro, then 19, had been waiting up for Luca, and it was he who received the frantic call from their mother, informing him that Luca had been rushed to the hospital with severe injuries. The memory of that night is etched in Alessandro's mind like a series of photographs - the sound of his mother's panicked voice, the feeling of helplessness as he sped to the hospital, and the sight of Luca's battered body lying motionless on the ICU bed. In the months that followed, Alessandro became increasingly consumed by the need to protect himself and those around him from potential harm. He began to notice suspicious behavior in others - a stranger glancing at his family too long, a friend joking about violence - and would immediately go on high alert, his body tensing up as if ready to spring into action. Comments about family or loved ones being hurt would send him spiraling into dark thoughts of what could have been, and the sight of specific body parts - broken bones, cuts, or bruises - would transport him back to that terrible night. Alessandro tried to cope with these feelings by avoiding media coverage of similar events, switching off the TV whenever a violent crime story came on, and steering clear of online articles about attacks on innocent people. He couldn't bear the thought of being alone in a room or building, as if the absence of others would leave him vulnerable to some unseen threat. But despite these efforts, he found himself increasingly isolated - unable to work due to anxiety, his relationships with friends and family strained by his constant vigilance. As time went on, Alessandro began to turn his frustration inward, physically harming himself in an attempt to release the overwhelming feelings of guilt, anger, and fear that had taken up residence inside him. His sleep grew fitful, punctuated by sudden movements or noises that would jolt him awake, leaving him breathless and disoriented. He started experiencing flashbacks - vivid, visceral replays of that autumn night, complete with the scent of antiseptic and blood that seemed to cling to his nostrils even years later. Alessandro struggled to verbalize his memories of the event, as if the words themselves might unleash a fresh wave of pain. When he did try to talk about it, the images came flooding back - Luca's swollen face, the beeping machines in the ICU, the numb feeling that had settled over him like a shroud. Alessandro felt like his body was working against him, perpetually on high alert even when logic told him he was safe. He'd lost faith in himself, unable to shake the conviction that he was no longer capable of protecting those he loved or doing the things that once defined him. His mind had become a constant battlefield, with fears and doubts vying for dominance. Lately, Alessandro's marriage has begun to suffer under the weight of his anxiety and withdrawal. His wife, tired of walking on eggshells around him, has started to feel like she's losing her partner to this sea of PTSD symptoms. It was her gentle insistence that he seek help that finally brought Alessandro to therapy - a step he hopes will lead him out of this darkness and back into the world of the living. For now, though, he remains trapped in this never-ending cycle of fear, his mind whispering an insistent refrain: you're not safe, you'll never be safe again.
